arXiv:2507.21797v2 [math.AP] 27 Feb 2026

Travelling front solutions in a spatially heterogeneous reaction-diffusion system

M. Chirilus-Bruckner*    L. van Vianen*    F. Veerman Note: Mathematical Institute, Leiden University, Einsteinweg 55, 2333 CC, Leiden, the Netherlands
Abstract

We investigate a two-component reaction-diffusion system with a slow-fast structure and spatially varying coefficients f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} appearing in the slow equation. Under mild boundedness and regularity conditions on f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} the system is shown to exhibit bi-stability in the form of two stable stationary heterogeneous background states. These background states can be connected by stationary and travelling front solutions. Travelling fronts feature an interface that moves with a non-uniform speed through the motionless spatially varying background states it connects. We construct both the background states and stationary fronts using an extension of Fenichel theory to the non-compact case. Additionally, we establish the existence of travelling front solutions and derive a leading-order expression for the dynamic position of the moving interface through a time-dependent spatial dynamics approach. This expression takes the form of a delay-differential equation, and its accuracy is validated through numerical simulations. A key contribution of our work lies in the general treatment of f1f_{1} and f2f_{2}, which are neither (necessarily) asymptotically small nor restricted to specific forms such as periodic or localized structures. Furthermore, our derivation of the front position formula circumvents the traditional reliance on spectral analysis, enabling us to describe front dynamics beyond bifurcations from stationary fronts. This approach has the potential to be extended to other settings in which spectral properties at onset preclude conventional reduction techniques.

1.1 Main results and Plan of the paper

The first main contribution is to prove that, under the mild Assumptions 1.1, the PDE admits two stable stationary heterogeneous background states (ub±​(x,ε),vb±​(x,ε))(u_{b}^{\pm}(x;\varepsilon),v_{b}^{\pm}(x;\varepsilon)). Their rigorous construction is sketched in Section 2. Adopting a spatial-dynamics viewpoint, we analyse the steady-state ODE, augmented by the additional variable χx=1\chi_{x}=1, which features critical and slow manifolds that are non-compact. We sketch an extension of classical Fenichel theory to the non-compact setting and prove the existence of two bounded solutions that correspond to the two heterogeneous background states in the PDE, which are shown in [39] to be stable.

The second main contribution, given in Section 3, is existence theory for front solutions connecting these motionless backgrounds. Stationary fronts are obtained in Section 3.1 as heteroclinic connections between the two bounded solutions of the steady-state ODE from Section 2, using a Melnikov-type computation that yields a leading-order existence and selection condition fixing admissible front locations, reflecting the loss of translation invariance caused by heterogeneity. Building on this, we further establish in Section 3.2 the existence of genuinely travelling fronts whose interface moves with non-uniform speed through stationary heterogeneous tails given by the heterogeneous background states from Section 2. We sketch the rather lengthy rigorous construction from [39], in which one first controls the initial-value problem with carefully defined “initialised fronts” and then tracks the evolution of the time derivatives (∂sU,∂sV)(\partial_{s}U,\partial_{s}V), which decay to zero in the far field since the backgrounds do not move. We round off our exposition with Section 4, where we derive a reduced law for the motion of the interface of travelling front solutions. In the singular limit ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, the front position z⁡(s)z(s) satisfies a delay-differential equation in which the instantaneous drift z′​(s)z^{\prime}(s) depends on a history-dependent functional W⁡[z]W[z] arising from solving an auxiliary linear parabolic problem for the slow field. Crucially, this reduction is obtained without spectral analysis, allowing front-dynamics descriptions beyond bifurcations from stationary fronts. Numerical simulations validate the leading-order delay law and illustrate regimes including heterogeneous speed modulation, attraction and repulsion by stationary fronts for α<0\alpha<0, and exploratory dynamics outside the strict assumptions.

Throughout this paper, we present the main results from [39] as ‘Results’ rather than ‘Theorems’, as this paper does not contain the proof of those results. All Results presented here correspond to Theorems in [39], whose proof can be found therein.

1.3 Related work and novelty of the present work

The transition from (1.2) to (1.1) is motivated by prior work on a related reaction-diffusion equation, namely, the extended Klausmeier model with spatially varying coefficients, which is used to model the dynamics of vegetation patterns in semi-arid regions where the spatially varying coefficients account for the change in topography (cf. [3]). This further generalised previous studies which assumed the terrain to be either flat or with a constant slope ([32]). The novelty in [3] consisted in using a blend of Geometric Singular Perturbation Theory (GSPT) and the theory of exponential dichotomies to construct spatially varying background states and stationary pulse solutions that are bi-asymptotic to those for x→±∞x\rightarrow\pm\infty. These new types of pulse solutions with heterogeneous tails model vegetation patches on varying topography. Going beyond the stationary case, a reduced description of the position of travelling vegetation patterns was given consisting of a coupled ODE-algebraic system that described the drift instability of stationary pulses. While similar in methodology to [3], the study of front solutions of (1.1) in the present work poses several new challenges whose resolution will allow to generalize the approach to a larger class of equations. We will comment on those throughout the text.

Going beyond the dynamics of single vegetation patches, the influence of heterogeneity on NN-pulse (also sometimes called NN-spike) solutions has been studied by a reduction procedure to a finite-dimensional systems of ODEs, e.g. in [5] and [23]. Furthermore, the limit of small-amplitude vegetation patterns on spatially periodic terrains has been studied in paradigm models such as the Swift-Hohenberg equation [27, 21] by deriving a Ginzburg-Landau equation for the pattern amplitude. In [28] even the idea of reversing desertification via resonance with a spatially periodic forcing coefficient was presented.

For scalar Nagumo/Allen-Cahn-type settings, in [29] and [4] the influence of heterogeneity on front and multi-front solutions has been studied. Related results can be also found in [31] for the Allen-Cahn with forcing and discrete versions thereof. Going back to reaction-diffusion systems, in [37] a three-component model of the form (1.2) was studied with γ=γ⁡(x)\gamma=\gamma(x) a step function. All of these settings can be viewed as complementary results to the present work, since they explain how heterogeneity influences primarily the fast variable UU.

The influence of heterogeneity on pattern formation in 2-D is a very active research field with many applications including to universal phenomena like the formation of Turing patterns or spiral waves. We refrain from giving an extensive list, but rather point to two bodies of work that contain a wealth of analytical results and techniques: [22], [17], [19], [18], [20] and also [35],[25], [24]. All these settings have many similarities with (1.1) and will serve as an inspiration for future work.

The proof of this result follows the steps taken in [15], in particular using the Hadamard graph transform, where uniform estimates obtained therein from the compactness of the underlying critical manifold are replaced by uniform estimates on the vector field (2.5). The proof of smoothness in ε\varepsilon (see [39, Chapter 3] for full details) follows the approach of [13], in particular Theorem 6 therein. These persistence results provide us with the existence of a function u±​(v,q,χ,ε)=±1+𝒪⁡(ε)u^{\pm}(v,q,\chi;\varepsilon)=\pm 1+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) parametrising the uu-component of ℳε±\mathcal{M}^{\pm}_{\varepsilon} as a graph over (v,q,χ)(v,q,\chi), which can be used to study the slow dynamics on ℳε±\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}^{\pm}, given by

vx\displaystyle v_{x} =q,\displaystyle=q, (2.11a)
qx\displaystyle q_{x} =(1+f1​(χ))​v−(1+f2​(χ))​u±​(v,q,χ,ε),\displaystyle=(1+f_{1}(\chi))v-(1+f_{2}(\chi))u^{\pm}(v,q,\chi;\varepsilon), (2.11b)
χx\displaystyle\chi_{x} =1.\displaystyle=1. (2.11c)

The results on nonlinear exponential dichotomies by Fenichel [16] can now be used to prove that the slow stable and unstable manifolds Ws​l​o​wu/s​(BO0±)W^{u/s}_{slow}(\text{BO}^{\pm}_{0}) perturb C1C_{1}-smoothly (w.r.t. the dynamics (2.11)), and that their transversal intersection BOε,R±\textnormal{BO}_{\varepsilon,R}^{\pm} is a C1C_{1}-smooth perturbation of the reduced singular bounded orbit BO0,R±\text{BO}^{\pm}_{0,R}. In addition, the (perturbed) manifolds Wslowu​(BOε±)⊆ℳε±W^{u}_{\text{slow}}(\text{BO}^{\pm}_{\varepsilon})\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}^{\pm} and Wslows​(BOε±)⊆ℳε±W^{s}_{\text{slow}}(\text{BO}^{\pm}_{\varepsilon})\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}^{\pm} are the stable and unstable manifolds of BOε,R±\textnormal{BO}_{\varepsilon,R}^{\pm} in the sense of Fenichel (w.r.t. the dynamics (2.11)). We obtain the background orbits BOε±\textnormal{BO}_{\varepsilon}^{\pm} in (2.5) as the image of BOε,R±\textnormal{BO}_{\varepsilon,R}^{\pm} under the inclusion map ℳε±↪ℝ5\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}^{\pm}\xhookrightarrow{}\mathbb{R}^{5}. The resulting geometry is similar to that in the singular limit; now, the intersection of Wslowu/s​(BOε±)W^{u/s}_{\text{slow}}(\text{BO}^{\pm}_{\varepsilon}) with the hyperplane {χ=χ0}\left\{\chi=\chi_{0}\right\} is a Fenichel fibre ℱu/s,±​(χ0)\mathcal{F}^{u/s,\pm}(\chi_{0}), see also Figure 3. The (u,v)(u,v)-components of the perturbed background orbits BOε±\text{BO}^{\pm}_{\varepsilon} correspond to the bounded stationary background states whose existence and properties are stated in Result 2.1.

Remark 2.5.

Already foreshadowing the construction of stationary front solutions via Melnikov analysis, we want to emphasise that in the compact case it is sufficient to have that Wu/s​(ℳ0±)W^{u/s}(\mathcal{M}_{0}^{\pm}) is a C2C^{2}-smooth perturbation to ensure C1C^{1}-smoothness of the Melnikov function. In the non-compact case one needs to go a step further and demand bounded C3C^{3}-smoothness which then implies uniform C2C^{2}-smoothness without compactness.

Remark 2.6.

In [39] is it shown that the background solutions from Result 2.1 are stable, hence, making (1.1) a bi-stable PDE.

Remark 2.7.

In the present equation setting the critical and slow manifold are different. This is in contrast with the corresponding system in [3] where the critical and slow manifold coincide. In that respect, the setting studied here is more representative of the general case.

3 Front solutions

While the concept of a travelling front is intuitively unambiguous, it turns out to be useful to provide a formal description of a travelling front solution to (1.1), as the presence of spatial heterogeneities introduces non-trivial spatio-temporal features to such solutions.

Definition 3.1 (Front solutions).

Let (ub±,vb±)(u_{b}^{\pm},v_{b}^{\pm}) be the stationary background states from Result 2.1. A front solution (UF,VF)\left(U_{\text{F}},V_{\text{F}}\right) is a bounded solution of (1.1) satisfying the following properties for all t∈Ψt\in\Psi where either Ψ=[t0,∞)\Psi=[t_{0},\infty) for some t0∈ℝt_{0}\in\mathbb{R} or Ψ=ℝ\Psi=\mathbb{R}:

  1. 1.

    (Regularity) (UF,VF)\left(U_{\text{F}},V_{\text{F}}\right) is C2C^{2}-smooth in xx and C1C^{1}-smooth in tt for t∈Ψt\in\Psi.

  2. 2.

    (Asymptotic behaviour in space) For every t∈Ψt\in\Psi, (UF​(⋅,t),VF​(⋅,t))\left(U_{\text{F}}(\cdot,t),V_{\text{F}}(\cdot,t)\right) is asymptotic to the stationary background states (ub±​(x),vb±​(x))(u_{b}^{\pm}(x),v_{b}^{\pm}(x)) as x→±∞x\to\pm\infty.

  3. 3.

    (Front interface properties) There exists an interval J:=[ul,ur]J:=[u_{l},u_{r}], ul<0<uru_{l}<0<u_{r} such that for all t∈Ψt\in\Psi

    1. (a)

      It:=UF−1​(⋅,t)​(J)I_{t}:=U_{\text{F}}^{-1}(\cdot,t)\left(J\right) is an interval,

    2. (b)

      UF​(⋅,t)U_{\text{F}}(\cdot,t) is a bijection between ItI_{t} and JJ,

    3. (c)

      0<inft∈Ψ​|It|0<\text{inf}_{t\in\Psi}\left|I_{t}\right| and supt∈Ψ​|It|<∞\text{sup}_{t\in\Psi}\left|I_{t}\right|<\infty, where |It|\left|I_{t}\right| is the length of the interval ItI_{t}.

  4. 4.

    (Uniform decay in tails) The decay of the solution at ±∞\pm\infty to the background states is uniform in t∈Ψt\in\Psi.

Definition 3.2 (Entire front solutions).

We call a front solution from Definition 3.1 an entire front if Ψ=ℝ\Psi=\mathbb{R}.

The front interface properties described in Definition 3.1 characterise a travelling front solution by the fact that a clearly defined front connection between the two stationary background states persists for an open time interval Ψ⊂ℝ\Psi\subset\mathbb{R}. In particular, properties 3a and 3b specify that, for fixed tt, this front interface is a monotonically increasing graph over an xx-interval ItI_{t}. Property 3c ensures that this interval persists in time, i.e. does not disappear or stretch to infinity. For a visual representation of Definition 3.1, see Figure 4.Note that Definition 3.1 confines our analysis to fronts that are left asymptotic to (ub−,vb−)(u_{b}^{-},v_{b}^{-}) and right asymptotic to (ub+,vb+)(u_{b}^{+},v_{b}^{+}), for which the connecting front is monotonically increasing in xx. This choice has been made for clarity of presentation; fronts that are left asymptotic to (ub+,vb+)(u_{b}^{+},v_{b}^{+}) and right asymptotic to (ub−,vb−)(u_{b}^{-},v_{b}^{-}) can be analysed in an analogous manner.

While in the constant-coefficient case (1.2) it is taken for granted that uniformly travelling front solutions exist for all time, a similar result for (1.1) will require considerably more effort. In particular, it will turn out to be necessary to first treat the initial value problem (leading to Definition 3.5 where Ψ\Psi from Definition 3.1 is not ℝ\mathbb{R}) to then prove the existence of entire solutions as given in Definition 3.2.

3.1 Stationary front solutions

Definition 3.1 does not specify any temporal behaviour of travelling front solutions to (1.1): in particular, stationary front solutions fall within the class of solutions described in Definition 3.1. Although the main focus of this paper is on the existence of genuinely travelling fronts, i.e. those with non-trivial temporal behaviour, it is necessary to briefly treat the existence of stationary front solutions to (1.1), as these can serve as attractors for the front solutions to (1.1) that do evolve in time.

For f1=f2=0f_{1}=f_{2}=0 the leading order existence condition (3.1) reduces to (1.3). 3.2 Travelling fronts with non-zero speed

We now move to travelling front solutions with with non-zero speed. We will formulate all results for the special case f1=0f_{1}=0. Similarly as for stationary fronts, the case f1≠0f_{1}\neq 0 is only more technical but does not need new techniques. A first step in the construction of travelling entire fronts is a solid command of the initial value problem for travelling fronts. Since this is of interest in its own right, we give a separate definition of initialised fronts.

Definition 3.5 (Initialised front solutions).

We call a front solution (UF,VF)(U_{F},V_{F}) from Definition 3.1 with initial condition (UF,VF)​(x,t0)=(U0,V0)​(x)(U_{F},V_{F})(x,t_{0})=(U_{0},V_{0})(x) for some t0∈ℝt_{0}\in\mathbb{R} an initialised front if Ψ=[t0,∞)\Psi=[t_{0},\infty).

We now set out to construct front solutions as in Definition 3.1 with a non-uniformly moving interface connecting motionless background states. We will work with the fast-reaction scaling (1.4) which is equivalent to (1.1). As alluded to, it will turn out to be useful to consider the linear PDE system that governs the dynamics of ∂sU\partial_{s}U and ∂sV\partial_{s}V, given by

{ε2​∂s(∂sU)=ε2​∂x2(∂sU)+(1−3​U2)​∂sU−ε​α​∂sV,τ^​∂s(∂sV)=∂x2(∂sV)−∂sV+(1+f2​(x))​∂sU.\left\{\begin{aligned} \varepsilon^{2}\partial_{s}\left(\partial_{s}U\right)&=\varepsilon^{2}\partial_{x}^{2}\left(\partial_{s}U\right)+(1-3U^{2})\partial_{s}U-\varepsilon\alpha\,\partial_{s}V,\\ {\hat{\tau}}\partial_{s}\left(\partial_{s}V\right)&=\partial_{x}^{2}\left(\partial_{s}V\right)-\partial_{s}V+(1+f_{2}(x))\partial_{s}U.\end{aligned}\right. (3.10)

System (3.10) can be used to determine the signs of ∂s2U\partial^{2}_{s}U and ∂s2V\partial^{2}_{s}V using similar arguments as in earlier steps of the proof. A crucial part is writing ∂sU\partial_{s}U as the sum of three parts: a ‘fade out’ part, which decreases exponentially in time; an ‘interface’ part, whose properties are determined by the shape of the front interface, and a ‘tails’ part, whose properties are determined by the asymptotic convergence to the background states. For all three parts, the variation of constants formula applied to (3.10) is used to establish estimates on |∂sU||\partial_{s}U|.

Positive feedback α<0\alpha<0

The aforementioned generic regularity results form the basis for the next step of the proof. When α<0\alpha<0, the set of functions (U0,V0)(U_{0},V_{0}) obeying properties 1, 2, 3, 6 and the additional property

  1. 10.

    ub−​(x)≤U0​(x)≤ub+​(x)u_{b}^{-}(x)\leq U_{0}(x)\leq u_{b}^{+}(x) and vb−​(x)≤V0​(x)≤vb+​(x)v_{b}^{-}(x)\leq V_{0}(x)\leq v_{b}^{+}(x)

can be shown to be forward invariant under the flow of (1.1), using integral estimates combined with repeatedly extending the length of finite time interval on which the results are shown to hold. In the next step, the front properties 4 and 5 are incorporated, together with the propagation direction property

  1. 11.

    U0(1)​(x,0),V0(1)​(x,0)≤0U_{0}^{(1)}(x,0),V_{0}^{(1)}(x,0)\leq 0 for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} and U0(1)​(x,0),V0(1)​(x,0)<0U_{0}^{(1)}(x,0),V_{0}^{(1)}(x,0)<0 for x∈I=U0−1​([uℓ,ur])x\in I=U_{0}^{-1}([u_{\ell},u_{r}]).

It can be shown that the these properties are forward invariant under the flow of (1.1).

Mixed feedback α>0\alpha>0

When α>0\alpha>0, the feedback of VV on UU in (1.1) is negative, while the feedback of UU on VV remains positive. This mixed feedback has profound impact on the dynamics of travelling fronts in (1.1). Indeed, when α>0\alpha>0, the propagation direction of the front might reverse; see also Example 2 in section 4.3. A related phenomenon is that, for α>0\alpha>0, the UU-component might overshoot the background states ub±u_{b}^{\pm}, in contrast to the travelling front described in Results 4.1 and 3.10.

We will now set out to formulate an existence result for α>0\alpha>0 for front solutions that travel in one fixed direction. We formulate two results on the existence of initialised travelling fronts in the absence of stationary fronts. The results are formulated for right-travelling fronts for clarity of presentation; results on left-travelling front can be obtained in an analogous manner.

Result 3.6.

Let α>0\alpha>0 and supx∈ℝd​vb−d​x​(x,0)<γα\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\frac{\mathrm{d}v_{b}^{-}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x;0)<\frac{\gamma}{\alpha}. and U0(1)≤λ0ε for x∈[U0−1(−1/3)−εd¯,U0−1(1/3)+εd¯],\displaystyle\text{and }U_{0}^{(1)}\leq\frac{\lambda_{0}}{\varepsilon}\text{ for }x\in\left[U_{0}^{-1}\left(-1/\sqrt{3}\right)-\varepsilon\underline{d},U_{0}^{-1}\left(1/\sqrt{3}\right)+\varepsilon\underline{d}\right], (3.12)

we have for the solution (U,V)(U,V) of the corresponding initial value problem for (1.1) that

(U⁡(⋅,s),V⁡(⋅,s))∈Γ→​(θ1,θ^2)for alls>s0.\left(U(\cdot,s),V(\cdot,s)\right)\in\Gamma^{\rightarrow}(\theta_{1},\widehat{\theta}_{2})\quad\text{for all}\quad s>s_{0}\,. (3.13)

Remark 3.7.

In case the assumptions on the initial conditions are relaxed from having compact support to being sufficiently localised in space, a similar result can be formulated with the addition that the front will be formed after a short initial calibration phase that is of order 𝒪⁡(ε2)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{2}) in ss (or equivalently order 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) in tt).

Proof strategy for mixed feedback α>0\alpha>0

[39, Chapter 4] When α>0\alpha>0, both boundedness between the background states (property 10.) and uniform direction of propagation (property 11.) are, in contrast to the positive feedback case, not forward invariant under the flow of (1.1). As a result, crucial building blocks that were used in the proof of Results 3.9 and 3.10 are missing.
However, the existence of an initialised travelling front – i.e. a solution that maintains its front shape and has a uniform propagation direction for all s>s0s>s_{0} – can for α>0\alpha>0 be shown using estimates on ∂sU\partial_{s}U based on the variation of constants formula applied to (3.10). The assumption supx∈ℝd​vb−d​x​(x,0)<γα\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\frac{\mathrm{d}v_{b}^{-}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x;0)<\frac{\gamma}{\alpha} is crucial, implying that the integral ∫z⁡(s)−εz⁡(s)+ε∂sU⁡(x,s)​d​x\int_{z(s)-\sqrt{\varepsilon}}^{z(s)+\sqrt{\varepsilon}}\partial_{s}U(x,s)\,\text{d}x is negative and uniformly bounded away from zero. Next, ∂sU\partial_{s}U is again written as the sum of three parts: a ‘fade out’ part, which decreases exponentially in time; an ‘interface’ part, whose properties are determined by the shape of the front interface, and a ‘tails’ part, whose properties are determined by the asymptotic convergence to the background states. The assumption of compact support (Result 3.6) or the assumption of initial calibration (Result 3.7) can now be used to estimate the integral of ∂sU\partial_{s}U in an ε\varepsilon-neighbourhood around the front position z⁡(s)z(s). Together with estimates on the ‘fade out’ part and the ‘tails’ part of ∂sU\partial_{s}U, this provides a bound of the form ∂sU<−λε\partial_{s}U<-\frac{\lambda}{\varepsilon} for some λ>0\lambda>0 for finite ss. Next, the uniformity of the obtained estimates can be used to extend the ss-interval of existence to all s≥s0s\geq s_{0}, thereby proving the existence of initialised travelling front solutions to (1.4).

3.2.2 Entire travelling front solutions

To make statements about the properties of travelling fronts with nonzero speed, it is necessary to define what we mean by "position":

The position of an entire travelling front (UTF,VTF)(U_{\text{TF}},V_{\text{TF}}) is defined as the unique function z⁡(s)z(s) for which UTF​(z​(s),s)=0U_{\text{TF}}(z(s),s)=0 for all s∈ℝs\in\mathbb{R}.

The starting point is to borrow intuition from the constant coefficient case when f2=0f_{2}=0. 4.2 Numerical algorithm for the delay-differential equation

Let s0s_{0} be an initial time and let z0∈PC1((−∞,s0])z_{0}\in\text{PC}^{1}((-\infty,s_{0}]) be a function specifying a ’history’. Consider the delay functional W⁡[z]W[z] given by (4.2) and the error term

e⁡(s,a):=23​z​[a]′​(s)−α⁡(τ^​W​[z⁡[a]]​(s)−qb−​(z⁡[a]​(s)),0)−γ,\displaystyle e(s,a):=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}z[a]^{\prime}(s)-\alpha(\hat{\tau}W[z[a]](s)-q_{b}^{-}(z[a](s));0)-\gamma,

i.e. the extended function z​[a]​(s)z[a](s) satisfies the delay differential equation at time ss if and only if e⁡(s,a)=0e(s,a)=0.

4.2.1 Algorithm 1

Input: An initial time s0s_{0} and a function z0∈PC1((−∞,s0])z_{0}\in\text{PC}^{1}((-\infty,s_{0}]) specifying a ’history’, such that z0​(s)z_{0}(s) satisfies the delay differential equation at s=s0s=s_{0}.   2. 2.

    We solve the equation ei​(si,a)=0e_{i}(s_{i},a)=0, for aa as follows. Existence and uniqueness of the solution a=ai∗a=a_{i}^{*} is justified in [39] for 0<h≪10<h\ll 1 (under suitable conditions on the history z^0(.)\widehat{z}_{0}(.) involving Lipschitz continuity, see [39]).

  3. 3.

    We define z^i∈PC1((−∞,si])\widehat{z}_{i}\in\text{PC}^{1}((-\infty,s_{i}]) by

    z^i:=z^i−1[ai∗]|(−∞,si]\displaystyle\widehat{z}_{i}:=\widehat{z}_{i-1}[a_{i}^{*}]|_{(-\infty,s_{i}]}

    By construction we have ei​(si,ai∗)=0e_{i}(s_{i},a_{i}^{*})=0, which means that z^i​(s)\widehat{z}_{i}(s) satisfies the delay differential equation at s=sis=s_{i}.

Output. Set z^:=z^N\widehat{z}:=\widehat{z}_{N}. Then (since ei​(si,ai∗)=0e_{i}(s_{i},a_{i}^{*})=0 for all ii by construction), z^​(s)\widehat{z}(s) solves the delay differential equation at s=sis=s_{i}, for i=0,…,Ni=0,\ldots,N.

In order to implement the algorithm one needs a way to efficiently compute numerically the double integral involved in the delay differential equation. To this end we use the following probabilistic interpretation

W⁡[z]​(s)=𝔼X∼Exp​(1)R|X∼Levy​(0,τ^​X22)​[1τ^​X​z′​(s−R)​(1+f2​(z⁡(s−R)))​Rexp⁡(−[1τ^+τ^4​(z⁡(s)−z⁡(s−R)R)2]​R)2​cosh⁡(12​τ^​(z⁡(s)−z⁡(s−R)R)​X)].\displaystyle W[z](s)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\text{Exp}(1)\atop R|X\sim\text{Levy}\left(0,\frac{\hat{\tau}X^{2}}{2}\right)}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\frac{1}{\hat{\tau}X}z^{\prime}(s-R)(1+f_{2}(z(s-R)))R\\ \exp\left(-\left[\frac{1}{\hat{\tau}}+\frac{\hat{\tau}}{4}\left(\frac{z(s)-z(s-R)}{R}\right)^{2}\right]R\right)\\ 2\cosh\left(\frac{1}{2}\hat{\tau}\left(\frac{z(s)-z(s-R)}{R}\right)X\right)\end{array}\right].

The probabilistic interpretation can be used to compute the double integral by means of using Monte Carlo integration. The main parameters determining the precision of the algorithm are the number of Monte Carlo samples MM per time steps, and the length of each time step hh (i.e. the temporal discretization) or equivalently, the temporal resolution R=⌈1h⌉R=\lceil\frac{1}{h}\rceil, i.e. the number of steps per unit time. Note that the computation time is 𝒪⁡(M​R)\mathcal{O}(MR).

4.2.3 Algorithm 1 vs Algorithm 2

It is good to keep both Algorithm 1 and Algorithm 2 because they provide two genuinely different numerical routes to the same reduced front-position law, and that difference is useful rather than redundant. Algorithm 1 works directly with the explicit delay functional W⁡[z]W[z] and typically evaluates the defining double integral via its probabilistic (Monte–Carlo) interpretation, whereas Algorithm 2 uses the implicit formulation by evolving the auxiliary field VRV_{R} through a PDE and coupling it back into the update of the position. Since these approaches have different sources of numerical error—Algorithm 1 is dominated by sampling variance (and time-stepping error), while Algorithm 2 is dominated by deterministic discretization and solver choices—keeping both provides an internal consistency check: when they agree (as in Example 0), this strongly supports both the reduction and the implementation. When they disagree (as in Example 3), the discrepancy is equally informative because it highlights parameter regimes in which one formulation or its discretization is more delicate, thereby aiding diagnosis of instability, stiffness, boundary effects, or insufficient resolution. Finally, the two methods offer complementary practical trade-offs: Algorithm 1 avoids building a full PDE solver and is convenient when one only needs z⁡(s)z(s), while Algorithm 2 can be efficient in some regimes, avoids Monte–Carlo sampling entirely, and simultaneously produces VR​(⋅,s)V_{R}(\cdot,s), which is useful for interpreting and validating the front dynamics.

4.3 Numerical exploration of front dynamics

We can now compare the dynamics predicted by the delay equation with direct simulations of the full PDE and explore several qualitatively different regimes. Example 0 considers a front in a heterogeneous medium without stationary fronts and shows how the heterogeneity modulates the front speed while preserving its direction of motion. Example 1 treats the case α<0\alpha<0 with two stationary fronts and illustrates how travelling fronts connect and interact with these equilibria in agreement with Results 3.9 and 3.10. Example 2 focuses on the homogeneous case f2≡0f_{2}\equiv 0 with mixed feedback α>0\alpha>0 and demonstrates direction-reversing fronts that connect different constant-speed travelling waves. Finally, Example 3 introduces a strong localized heterogeneity (outside the rigorous assumptions) that acts as a pair of “direction switches” and leads to numerically observed periodic front motion, providing an exploratory test of the delay equation beyond the theoretical setting. The corresponding code is avaiable at [40].

Example 0: Travelling front moving with a time-dependent speed z′​(s)z^{\prime}(s) in the absence of stationary fronts.

We consider a compactly supported f2f_{2}. The front enters and passes through the support of f2f_{2}. We set α=0.5\alpha=0.5, γ=0.2\gamma=0.2, τ^=1\hat{\tau}=1. We define f2​(x)f_{2}(x) as a piecewise polynomial defined on [−3,15][-3,15]. To this end, we sample the function

(y−3)​sin⁡(1+14​(y−3)3)​exp⁡(−1.2​|y−3|)\displaystyle(y-3)\sin\!\bigl(1+14(y-3)^{3}\bigr)\exp\!\bigl(-1.2|y-3|\bigr)

for the yy-values y=3,4,5,6,7,8,9y=3,4,5,6,7,8,9 and then use MATLAB’s makima interpolation to construct a piecewise polynomial defined on [3,10][3,10] satisfying f2​(3)=f2​(10)=0f_{2}(3)=f_{2}(10)=0. The sampled values y=4,5,6,7,8,9y=4,5,6,7,8,9 (approximately) specify the local minima and maxima of the resulting f2f_{2}. For x≤3x\leq 3 and x≥10x\geq 10 we set f2​(x)=0f_{2}(x)=0.

When f2=0f_{2}=0, there exists a unique constant-speed travelling front. In the singular limit, the speed is given by c≈0.83c\approx 0.83. Introducing f2f_{2}, we expect that outside the support of f2f_{2} the dynamics are close to the dynamics of the constant-coefficient model; in particular, the singular limit of the front velocity will be close to 0.830.83. We simulate the PDE for various values of 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1 (using MATLAB’s pdepe), with an initial condition (U0,V0)(U_{0},V_{0}) starting at position z0=−2.5z_{0}=-2.5 (outside the support of f2f_{2}). That is, z0=−2.5z_{0}=-2.5 is the starting position, in the sense that U0​(z0)=0U_{0}(z_{0})=0. The initial condition is constructed by first simulating the constant-coefficient PDE. The fronts travel to the right with positive speed, and pass through the support of f2f_{2}. The front speed remains positive, but is not constant and fluctuates when the front is in the vicinity of the support of f2f_{2}.

Example 1: Travelling front for α<0\alpha<0 in the presence of stationary fronts.

The aim of the present example is to illustrate Result 3.10, describing the interaction of travelling fronts and stationary fronts for positive feedback α<0\alpha<0. To this end we consider the parameter values α=−2\alpha=-2, γ=−0.2\gamma=-0.2, τ^=1\hat{\tau}=1, and

f2​(x)=0.3​exp⁡(−0.5​(x+0.1)2)+0.33​exp⁡(−2​(x+1.5)2)−0.53​exp⁡(−2​(x+0.75)2)+0.25​exp⁡(−4​(x−0.1)2)−0.4​exp⁡(−3​(x−1)2).\displaystyle\begin{split}f_{2}(x)=&0.3\exp(-0.5(x+0.1)^{2})+0.33\exp(-2(x+1.5)^{2})-0.53\exp(-2(x+0.75)^{2})\\ &+0.25\exp(-4(x-0.1)^{2})-0.4\exp(-3(x-1)^{2})\,.\end{split} (4.30)

For 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1, there exist two stationary fronts SFi​(ε)\textnormal{SF}_{i}(\varepsilon) with positions z0,i​(ε)z_{0,i}(\varepsilon), i=1,2i=1,2, where by Result 3.3 the singular limit positions z0,i​(0)z_{0,i}(0) are given by the solutions z0z_{0} of the equation qb−​(z0,0)=γα=0.1q_{b}^{-}(z_{0};0)=\frac{\gamma}{\alpha}=0.1. Approximately, we have z0,1​(0)≈0.38z_{0,1}(0)\approx 0.38 and z0,2​(0)≈0.90z_{0,2}(0)\approx 0.90. The stationary front at position z0,1​(ε)z_{0,1}(\varepsilon) is unstable (since (qb−)′​(z0,1​(0),δ0,0)>0(q_{b}^{-})^{\prime}(z_{0,1}(0);\delta_{0},0)>0) and the stationary front at position z0,2​(ε)z_{0,2}(\varepsilon) is stable (see Result 3.10).

To generate an initial condition at a given target position z0∈ℝz_{0}\in\mathbb{R} (in particular in the vicinity of the unstable stationary front for ε>0\varepsilon>0), we use the following algorithm. Let z0∈ℝz_{0}\in\mathbb{R} be the target position where we want to construct an initial condition (U0,V0)(U_{0},V_{0}). Start with an initial condition (U0,0,V0,0)(U_{0,0},V_{0,0}) which has a front-like shape (i.e. connecting the background states and having a single interface). Taking a sequence (Ti)i(T_{i})_{i}, Ti>0T_{i}>0, we iteratively construct initial conditions (U0,i,V0,i)(U_{0,i},V_{0,i}) by solving the PDE (1.4) with initial condition (U0,i−1,V0,i−1)(U_{0,i-1},V_{0,i-1}) up to time TiT_{i}, and then shifting the resulting solution (U,V)i−1​(x,Ti)(U,V)_{i-1}(x,T_{i}) in space to the position z0z_{0}, i.e. (U0,i,V0,i)​(x):=(U,V)i−1​(x−z0+zi−1​(Ti),Ti)(U_{0,i},V_{0,i})(x):=(U,V)_{i-1}(x-z_{0}+z_{i-1}(T_{i}),T_{i}). The main idea is to let Ti→0T_{i}\to 0 while also ensuring that ∑iTi\sum_{i}T_{i} is not too small in order to filter out transient dynamics.

We choose to work with the following sequence of times T1=1T_{1}=1, T2=1T_{2}=1, T3=1T_{3}=1, T4=0.5T_{4}=0.5, T5=0.5T_{5}=0.5, T6=0.3T_{6}=0.3, T7=0.2T_{7}=0.2.

For ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05 we estimate that the position z0,1​(0.05)z_{0,1}(0.05) of the stationary front is contained in the interval [0.37577,0.37609][0.37577,0.37609]. The estimate arises from the fact that we constructed an initial condition (U0,a,V0,a)(U_{0,a},V_{0,a}) at position 0.375770.37577 which ends up generating a front travelling to the left, and an initial condition (U0,b,V0,b)(U_{0,b},V_{0,b}) at position 0.376090.37609 which generates a front travelling to the right. Likewise, for ε=0.1\varepsilon=0.1 we estimate that z0,1​(0.1)z_{0,1}(0.1) is contained in the interval [0.37714,0.38452][0.37714,0.38452].

The position of the stable stationary front is (surprisingly) a bit harder to estimate. On the one hand, stability implies that approaching fronts from the right and left are attracted, and consequently it appears that the position can be estimated in this way by tracking approaching fronts numerically for long enough. However, the numerics involve a discretization of space, and the position of the numerical front is confined to this grid. Hence, to estimate the position of the stationary front more precisely, one needs to increase the resolution of the grid, which quickly increases computation time.

Figure 9 and Figure 10 illustrate a travelling front connecting stationary fronts SF1\textnormal{SF}_{1} in backward time and SF2\textnormal{SF}_{2} in forward time. Both the position z⁡(s)z(s) and the front velocity z′​(s)z^{\prime}(s) closely agree with the associated singular position and velocity given by simulating the delay-differential equation. In particular, when looking only at the front position z⁡(s)z(s) (Figure 10), the comparison between ε=0.1\varepsilon=0.1 and ε=0\varepsilon=0 is already remarkably precise, which is why ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05 is not included in this figure. On the other hand, the comparison for the front velocity z′​(s)z^{\prime}(s) with the delay-differential equation (Figure 9) noticeably improves for ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05 compared to ε=0.1\varepsilon=0.1. Figures 11 and Figure 12 extend the simulation by including other travelling fronts besides the travelling front connecting the stationary fronts. Specifically, a travelling front is included which travels away from the unstable stationary front SF1\textnormal{SF}_{1} to the left, and a travelling front which approaches the stable stationary front SF2\textnormal{SF}_{2} from the right.

Example 2: Direction-reversing front for α>0\alpha>0 and f2=0f_{2}=0.

We set τ^=1\hat{\tau}=1, γ=0.2\gamma=0.2. Let αbp\alpha_{\textnormal{bp}} be given by

αb​p=(23​cb​p−γ)​4+cb​p2​τ^2cb​p​τ^≈1.489,cb​p=−(12​γ2​τ^2)13.\displaystyle\alpha_{bp}=\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}c_{bp}-\gamma\right)\frac{\sqrt{4+c_{bp}^{2}\hat{\tau}^{2}}}{c_{bp}\hat{\tau}}\approx 1.489\,,\quad c_{bp}=-\left(\frac{12\gamma}{\sqrt{2}\hat{\tau}^{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}\,. (4.31)

For α<αb​p\alpha<\alpha_{bp}, the algebraic equation (4.10) has a unique solution cc which corresponds to (up to translation in space) a unique constant-speed travelling front for the PDE (1.4) for 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1. For α>αb​p\alpha>\alpha_{bp}, (4.10) has three solutions cm<c0<cpc_{m}<c_{0}<c_{p}, which for 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1 correspond to travelling fronts with speeds cm​(ε)<c0​(ε)<0<cp​(ε)c_{m}(\varepsilon)<c_{0}(\varepsilon)<0<c_{p}(\varepsilon).

For the present example, we take α=2.5>αb​p\alpha=2.5>\alpha_{bp}. We also fix ε=0.1\varepsilon=0.1 and compare it with the singular limit ε=0\varepsilon=0.

One can show that the delay-differential equation [39, Chapter 5] has an entire solution z⁡(s)z(s), which satisfies z′​(s)→c0<0z^{\prime}(s)\to c_{0}<0 as s→−∞s\to-\infty, z′​(s)→cp>0z^{\prime}(s)\to c_{p}>0 as s→∞s\to\infty, and z′​(s)z^{\prime}(s) is increasing in ss. That is, in the singular limit ε=0\varepsilon=0 there exists a travelling front which changes direction, i.e. it initially travels to the left with negative speed (asymptotic to c0c_{0} in backward time) and eventually approaches the positive speed cp>0c_{p}>0. In this example we explore numerically whether the PDE (1.4) has a similar direction-reversing travelling front solution for 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1 (approaching c0​(ε)c_{0}(\varepsilon) and cp​(ε)c_{p}(\varepsilon) in backward, respectively forward time).

For setting up the simulation, the main challenge is to construct the initial condition (U0,V0)(U_{0},V_{0}), which should be close to the front profile of the unstable constant-speed travelling front with speed c0​(ε)c_{0}(\varepsilon). To this end we consider the singularly perturbed system of ODEs for (u,p,v,q)(u,p,v,q) corresponding (in the fast scaling ξ\xi) to the co-moving frame ξ=x−c​sε\xi=\frac{x-cs}{\varepsilon}. For a given value of cc, there exists a unique orbit (standardized such that u⁡(0)=0u(0)=0), which is forward asymptotic to the (independent of xx, since in the present example f2=0f_{2}=0) background state (ub+​(ε),0,ub+​(ε),0)(u_{b}^{+}(\varepsilon),0,u_{b}^{+}(\varepsilon),0) and a unique orbit which is backward asymptotic to (ub−​(ε),0,ub−​(ε),0)(u_{b}^{-}(\varepsilon),0,u_{b}^{-}(\varepsilon),0). For c=cm​(ε),c0​(ε),cp​(ε)c=c_{m}(\varepsilon),c_{0}(\varepsilon),c_{p}(\varepsilon), these forward and backward orbits match at z0=0z_{0}=0, and form a heteroclinic. We numerically determine the value c0​(ε)c_{0}(\varepsilon) which gives rise to a heteroclinic orbit. To this end we identify locally invariant manifolds ℳε±\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}^{\pm} and restrict first to the one-parameter family of orbits which lie in the intersection of Wu​(ℳε−)W^{u}(\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}^{-}) and Ws​(ℳε+)W^{s}(\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}^{+}). To find this family of orbits we use an approximation of ℳε±\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}^{\pm} (the first order approximation in ε\varepsilon already works well), and a ‘shooting’ approach (tracking multiple orbits and investigating how closely they approach ℳε±\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}^{\pm}). The resulting family is described by u0=0u_{0}=0 and (p0,v0)(p_{0},v_{0}) being a function of qq. We then use a second layer of ‘shooting’ to investigate, for fixed cc, which forward orbit in (the one-parameter family) Ws​(ℳε−)∩Wu​(ℳε+)W^{s}(\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}^{-})\cap W^{u}(\mathcal{M}_{\varepsilon}^{+}) converges to the positive background state, and which backward orbit converges to the negative background state. Lastly, using a bisection approach we can compute the value of cc where the forward and backward orbits match. According to the numerical results, c0​(ε)c_{0}(\varepsilon) (for ε=0.1\varepsilon=0.1) is contained in the interval (−0.309375,−0.30875)(-0.309375,-0.30875) (for comparison the singular limit velocity is given by c0​(0)=−0.261792c_{0}(0)=-0.261792). We now consider the following cases.

To construct an initial condition (U0,V0)(U_{0},V_{0}) such that the solution of the PDE (1.4) will reverse the direction of travelling, we take cc slightly larger than c0​(ε)c_{0}(\varepsilon) and define (U0,V0)(U_{0},V_{0}) by means of concatenating the forward orbit converging to the positive background state with the backward orbit converging to the negative background state. How long the velocity z′​(s)z^{\prime}(s) stays close to c0​(ε)c_{0}(\varepsilon) before moving away from it depends on how close cc is to c0​(ε)c_{0}(\varepsilon), as well as on other numerical factors (i.e. in the shooting algorithm described above).

To construct an initial condition (U0,V0)(U_{0},V_{0}) for which the solution of the PDE will not reverse direction but instead converge to the stable travelling front with speed cm​(ε)c_{m}(\varepsilon), we take cc slightly smaller than c0​(ε)c_{0}(\varepsilon) and again concatenate forward and backward orbits.

For ε=0\varepsilon=0, we simulate the delay-differential equation, specifying the history to be z0=0z_{0}=0 and z′​(s)=c0​(0)z^{\prime}(s)=c_{0}(0) for s≤0s\leq 0. Using the Monte Carlo approach for evaluating the delay functional, it depends on the specific sample realizations (i.e. seed for the pseudo random number generator) whether the velocity z′​(s)z^{\prime}(s) ends up converging to cp​(0)c_{p}(0) or cm​(0)c_{m}(0). How long the solution of the delay-differential equation stays close to cm​(0)c_{m}(0) before splitting up depends (in particular) on the number of Monte Carlo samples, and the time discretization.

In summary, we obtain two numerical PDE solutions for ε=0.1\varepsilon=0.1, one which connects the velocities c0​(ε)<0c_{0}(\varepsilon)<0 and cp​(ε)>0c_{p}(\varepsilon)>0 (and in particular reverses its direction of travelling) and a second solution which connects the velocities c0​(ε)<0c_{0}(\varepsilon)<0 and cm​(ε)<0c_{m}(\varepsilon)<0. For ε=0\varepsilon=0 we obtain similar solutions of the delay-differential equation. Figures 13, 14, 15 depict the position and velocity compared for ε=0\varepsilon=0 and ε=0.1\varepsilon=0.1.

Example 3: Direction switches and periodic front.

A periodic front for the parameter values (α,γ,τ^)(\alpha,\gamma,\hat{\tau}) of Example 2 when the inhomogeneity f2f_{2} is introduced.

Unlike Examples 0 and 1, which illustrate theoretical results (i.e. Result 4.1 and Result 3.10, respectively), and Example 2 which illustrates partial results (i.e. the existence of direction-reversing entire solutions for the delay-differential equation (ε=0\varepsilon=0), but not for the PDE (1.4) for ε>0\varepsilon>0), the present example is purely exploratory (in the sense that it is not backed up by theoretical results). In fact the f2f_{2} which we will work with does not satisfy Assumptions 1.1.

The delay-differential equation is of the form

γ+α⁡(τ^​W​[z]​(s)−qb−​(z⁡(s),0))=23​z′​(s).\gamma+\alpha\bigl(\hat{\tau}W[z](s)-q_{b}^{-}(z(s);0)\bigr)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}z^{\prime}(s).

In particular, it appears that sudden large changes in qb−q_{b}^{-} might have a similar impact on the velocity z′​(s)z^{\prime}(s). This raises the question whether a localised inhomogeneity f2f_{2} might act as a ‘direction switch’, i.e. cause approaching fronts to reverse their direction.

We explore this question in the context of the parameters in Example 2, where we discussed that in the absence of f2f_{2} there exist stable speeds cm​(ε)<0c_{m}(\varepsilon)<0 and cp​(ε)>0c_{p}(\varepsilon)>0. We introduce the following f2f_{2} given by two localized pulses at positions z=±11z=\pm 11

f2​(x)=−ρ​exp⁡(−40​(x+11)2)−ρ​exp⁡(−40​(x−11)2).\displaystyle f_{2}(x)=-\rho\exp(-40(x+11)^{2})-\rho\exp(-40(x-11)^{2})\,. (4.32)

We set ρ=12\rho=12. The graph of the corresponding qb−​(⋅,0)q_{b}^{-}(\cdot;0) has large changes in the vicinity of positions z=±11z=\pm 11 of the pulses and is close to 00 everywhere else.

Near z0=0z_{0}=0 (far away from ±11\pm 11) we expect the front dynamics to be close to the constant-coefficient model where f2=0f_{2}=0. Consider a front travelling to the left away from z0=0z_{0}=0 with speed close to cm​(ε)<0c_{m}(\varepsilon)<0. This front approaches z=−11z=-11 from the right and will encounter the large negative local minimum of qb−q_{b}^{-}. Given the sudden decrease of qb−q_{b}^{-}, z′​(s)z^{\prime}(s) might quickly increase as a response, and if the drop in qb−q_{b}^{-} is large enough, z′​(s)z^{\prime}(s) might become positive, i.e. the front reverses direction.

Likewise, consider a front travelling to the right away from z0=0z_{0}=0 and towards z=11z=11 with speed close to cp​(ε)c_{p}(\varepsilon). This front will encounter the large local maximum of qb−q_{b}^{-}. Consequently, the front speed z′​(s)z^{\prime}(s) might decrease, and could become negative.

The numerical results confirm expectations. Figure 18 shows the simulated front position z⁡(s)z(s) against time and suggests that the pulses placed at positions z=±11z=\pm 11 act as direction switches as intended. The change of direction occurs around z=±10z=\pm 10. In particular, the front position is trapped in the compact interval [−11,11][-11,11]. A periodic front seems to emerge as a consequence of the two direction switches.

5 Summary and outlook

We have demonstrated that (1.1) exhibits bi-stability, characterized by two stable stationary background states that vary in space due to the presence of f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} and further give rise to stationary and travelling front solutions that connect them.

The construction of stationary background states in the stationary wave ODE (2.5) needed an extension of Fenichel theory to the general non-autonomous case (that is, going beyond [12] to include also unstable directions) combined with the theory of exponential dichotomies. Using a Melnikov-type argument for (2.5) gave also a leading order existence condition for stationary front solutions (3.1) that resembles the one for the constant-coefficient case (1.3), the difference being that, for fixed parameter settings, the possible front positions x0x_{0} are fixed (contrasting with the translation-invariant case of constant-coefficient equations). Travelling front solutions have a richer structure then their counterparts in the constant-coefficient case: their interfaces move non-uniformly through the motionless heterogeneous background states, which makes the usual travelling wave ansatz hopeless. Upon carefully defining them along their stationary version and numerical observations (see Definition 3.1), it turns out that one can prove (i) their existence from a specific set-up of the corresponding initial value problem (leading to initialised fronts as in Definition 3.5) and (ii) their existence for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} (leading to entire front solutions as in Definition 3.2). The main novelty of the proof for the IVP lies in tracking the time evolution of the time-derivatives (∂tU,∂tV)(\partial_{t}U,\partial_{t}V) which are bi-asymptotic to zero as x→±∞x\to\pm\infty for each fixed tt (since the background states are motionless even for travelling front solutions). The proof of the existence of entire solutions is built on the result for the IVP and uses the construction of a localised co-moving frame and the Arzela-Ascoli theorem. The exposition closes with a short formal derivation of a delay-differential equation (4.1) that describes the temporal evolution of the front position (in the sense of Definition 3.8). We briefly sketch a numerical algorithm to solve it and give various examples, both for cases where its validity can be proven rigorously and cases where its validity is expected but not proven. All proofs can be found in [39] and will also be subject of follow-up articles for which the present article serves as overview.

Future research will further generalize the obtained results to other settings with particular interest in treating also nonlinear slow equations, that is, the +U+U in the VV-equation in (1.1) replaced by F⁡(U,V)F(U,V). Furthermore, a careful study of the dynamics exhibited by the delay-differential equation (4.1) will be of interest, but is expected to be challenging due to the difficult type of delay differential equation. Another immediate question is its relation with the traditional approach of deriving reduced ODEs for the dynamic position using a rigorous center manifold reduction (CMR)(for a "collective coordinates type" approach). This is especially interesting since the derivation of (4.1) made no smallness assumption on zz, which one does when constructing travelling fronts as bifurcating from stationary ones. Note that, the conventional CMR approach for (1.1) would need control over the spectrum of the operator obtained from linearisation around stationary fronts. This is, in general, difficult unless one enforces smallness assumptions for f1,f2f_{1},f_{2} or assumes them to be periodic or spatially localised (as done in [3] for the stability of pulses). The derivation of the delay-differential equation completely circumvents this difficulty.

Further capitalising on the derivation of the delay-differential equation that avoids intricate spectral problems, a promising direction is to use this approach for interacting multi-front and pulse solutions under the influence of spatial heterogeneity. Going beyond the 1-D case, a promising direction is the study of 2-D front solutions and more complicated 2-D patterns such as the tracking of spiral wave tips in reaction-diffusion systems (as given, e.g. in [2, 1, 30, 41]) with applications, e.g. in the modelling of cardiac dynamics where heterogeneities are believed to play a major role.
